transcript:
This message comes from Schwab. At Schwab, you can get everything from self-directed investing to full-service wealth management, all in one place.
No matter your investing goal, life stage, amount to invest, or know-how, you can invest your way with Schwab.
This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Lyndi Kenyon. President Trump has changed his mind again and will now hold rallies in Kansas and Iowa.
NPR's Frank Ordonez reports.
The president had said earlier that he was canceling those visits because Republicans were in good shape in those states, but now he's taking a different tack.
We got a call from Iowa and from the people and from my friends that are very, very good. And we have a couple of races that are very important.
And they said if you could go, it would be better than a teller rally. And I tried to talk about that. I said, what about a teller rally?
But they asked me, so I'm going to do two on Sunday.
The president says he's not going on Saturday because of college football, but would leave early Sunday morning for Iowa and then head to Kansas.
Franco Ordonez, NPR News, The White House.
France's Interior Minister has warning there's a very high risk of violence and public disorder around protests planned for today.
As NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reports, the security presence at these protests will be massive.
70,000 police are expected on French streets, including elite units, as well as helicopters, drones, water cannon trucks and armored vehicles.
The French nightly news is full of the kind of videos that worry the government, social media posts calling on young people to come out in costumes and masks to party and some calling for chaos.
The confluence of Halloween with the protests has forced many cities to cancel Halloween celebrations and ban the sale of fireworks.
In Paris, where more than 100,000 demonstrators are expected in the streets, authorities are working to change the plan protest route to avoid the city center.
Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Paris.
A grand jury in Texas has indicted an ICE officer accused of intentionally hitting a Mexican construction worker with his car earlier this month.
The man was later placed in custody, suffering from a broken leg.
Houston Public Media's Bianca Seward reports.
Mario Alberto Morales was indicted for a second-degree felony offense of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.
Harris County District Attorney Shawn Tiers says he hopes the indictment will send a message.
An ICE badge does not give you free rein to injure, kill or violate the constitutional rights of anyone.
An ICE spokesperson claimed the victim, Miguel Parra Hernandez, ran in front of the agent's vehicle while they were trying to arrest a different man.
Parra Hernandez's lawyer has disputed ICE's account.
Surveillance video of the incident shows the agent driving towards Parra Hernandez as he runs away from the car and into a parking lot where the collision occurred.
For NPR News, I'm Bianca Seward in Houston.
The Congolese Ministry of Health reports deaths in Congo's Ebola outbreak have now topped 5,000.
More than 10,000 people have been infected.
The outbreak was declared in mid-May and is the second deadliest in history.
You're listening to NPR.
A new pair of blood tests can help doctors determine whether a patient may have Alzheimer's disease.
John Hamilton reports that the tests offer an alternative to expensive brain scans.
The blood tests measure a protein called PTOW 217.
It's closely associated with the presence of amyloid plaques in the brain, a hallmark of Alzheimer's.
Dr. David Holtzman of Washington University School of Medicine helped develop the approach.
That particular test is extremely accurate at determining whether you have amyloid in the brain or not.
Nearly as good as a costly PET scan.
Holtzman says the new blood tests are meant for older people who are already experiencing problems with memory and thinking, not people who are just curious about their brain health.
They were approved by the Food and Drug Administration this summer.
For NPR News, I'm John Hamilton.
After a brief bidding war, the manuscript map that helped divide the United States into North and South, free and slave states, has sold for $950,000.
Bidding started at $400,000, but curators had initially expected the map to fetch more than $1 million.
The map was finished in 1768 by Charles Mason and Jeremiah Dixon and determined what has become known as the Mason-Dixon Line.
Lauren Brunk of Brunk Auctions in Asheville, North Carolina says 45 bidders battled for just under three minutes to own that hand-drawn survey of the Mason-Dixon Line.
No word on who actually bought the map.
I'm Linda Kenyon, NPR News, in Washington.
For more information, visit voterready.iowa.gov, sponsored by Civic Futures Fund.

topics.text: Trump reverses course and will hold rallies in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday
France braces for nationwide protests with 70,000 police deployed and Halloween-related unrest feared
ICE officer indicted in Houston for allegedly hitting Mexican construction worker Miguel Parra Hernandez with car
Congo's Ebola outbreak deaths top 5,000, with over 10,000 infected, second deadliest ever
New blood tests can help doctors determine Alzheimer's disease risk, offering alternative to PET scans
Manuscript Mason-Dixon Line map sells for $950,000 at auction in Asheville, North Carolina
